questions.stem: The elbow joint is made of three diarthroses. Match each with its type:
options: Proximal radio-ulnar joint: plane joint
Humero-ulnar joint: trochlear joint
Humero-ulnar joint: trochoid joint
Proximal radio-ulnar joint: trochoid joint
Humero-radial joint: ball-and-socket (enarthrosis)
questions.explanation: Humero-ulnar = trochlear (flexion-extension); proximal radio-ulnar = trochoid (pronation-supination); humero-radial = enarthrosis, taking part in both.

questions.stem: Why is the elbow considered functionally a single joint?
options: They share a single ligamentous apparatus
They share a single synovial membrane
They are all trochlear joints
They all have separate capsules
Its three joints share a single joint cavity
questions.explanation: The three joints form one: one cavity, one synovial membrane, one ligamentous apparatus. They are of different types (trochlear, trochoid, enarthrosis).

questions.stem: About the articular surfaces of the distal humerus at the elbow:
options: The trochlea is surmounted anteriorly by the coronoid fossa
The radial fossa lies posterior to the capitulum
The trochlea is a segment of a spheroid
The capitulum is a segment of a spheroid
The olecranon fossa lies anteriorly above the trochlea
questions.explanation: The olecranon fossa is posterior, above the trochlea. Also false: "The trochlea is a segment of a spheroid"; "The radial fossa lies posterior to the capitulum".

questions.stem: The trochlear notch of the ulna:
options: Articulates with the capitulum
Is hook-shaped and fits onto the humeral trochlea
Has its two facets separated by a transverse groove
Has an anterior vertical facet formed by the olecranon
Has a posterior horizontal facet on the coronoid process
questions.explanation: The trochlear notch articulates with the trochlea; the capitulum articulates with the radial fovea. Also false: "Has a posterior horizontal facet on the coronoid process"; "Has an anterior vertical facet formed by the olecranon".

questions.stem: The radial notch of the ulna:
options: Is shaped like a hollow cylinder segment
Occupies the external face of the coronoid process
Articulates with the capitulum
Articulates with the articular circumference of the radial head
Occupies the medial face of the olecranon
questions.explanation: The radial notch is on the lateral (external) face of the coronoid process and receives the radial head's circumference.

questions.stem: The articular fovea of the radial head:
options: Is the superior, excavated surface of the radial head
Has a bevelled inner rim articulating with the capitulo-trochlear groove
Articulates with the trochlea
Articulates with the capitulum of the humerus
Articulates with the radial notch of the ulna
questions.explanation: The radial notch of the ulna receives the articular circumference, not the fovea.

questions.stem: The annular ligament of the radius:
options: Is a fibrocartilaginous band about 1 cm high
Its outer surface adheres to the articular capsule
Is both an articular surface and a passive ligament
Its inner surface is covered with articular cartilage
Extends from the anterior to the posterior border of the radial notch of the ulna
questions.explanation: Deep (inner) surface: articular, cartilage-covered, facing the radial head; superficial (outer) surface: fibrous, adhering to the capsule.

questions.stem: The radial head's circumference is enclosed in an osteofibrous ring formed by:
options: The olecranon
The radial notch of the ulna
The quadrate ligament
The annular ligament
The capitulum
questions.explanation: The osteofibrous ring = radial notch of the ulna + annular ligament.

options: Attaches on the inferior borders of the epicondyles
Inserts directly on the radial head cartilage
Is lined on its deep surface by the synovial membrane
Inserts on the radial neck about half a centimetre below the radial head
Runs along the superior border of the coronoid and radial fossae anteriorly
questions.explanation: On the radius, the capsule inserts on the neck, 0.5 cm below the head, not on the head itself.

questions.stem: The ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow:
options: Arises from the lateral epicondyle
Its posterior (Bardinet) bundle ends on the coronoid process
All its bundles arise from the medial epicondyle
Its arcuate (Cooper) bundle runs from the medial epicondyle to the radial neck
Is formed of anterior, middle and posterior bundles
questions.explanation: The ulnar collateral ligament arises from the medial epicondyle; the radial collateral ligament from the lateral epicondyle. Also false: "Its posterior (Bardinet) bundle ends on the coronoid process"; "Its arcuate (Cooper) bundle runs from the medial epicondyle to the radial neck".

questions.stem: Which bundle of the elbow ligaments is called Bardinet's bundle?
options: The posterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament
The posterior bundle of the radial collateral ligament
The horizontal humero-humeral bundles
The anterior oblique bundle of the anterior ligament
The arcuate bundle between the coronoid process and the olecranon
questions.explanation: Bardinet = fan-shaped posterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament (medial epicondyle → olecranon). The arcuate bundle is Cooper's ligament.

questions.stem: The radial collateral ligament of the elbow:
options: Its middle bundle ends on the radius, in front of the radial notch
Its posterior bundle ends on the radial neck
Arises from the lateral epicondyle
Ends on the radial head
Its anterior bundle ends at the radial notch
questions.explanation: All three bundles end on the ulna; none attaches to the radius (the only ligament attaching to the radius is the quadrate ligament). Also false: "Its posterior bundle ends on the radial neck"; "Its middle bundle ends on the radius, in front of the radial notch".

options: Is a bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament
Extends from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon
Extends from the inferior border of the radial notch to the medial part of the radial neck
Attaches to the radius
Is a quadrilateral plate
questions.explanation: The inferior (quadrate) ligament joins the ulna's radial notch to the radial neck.

questions.stem: Which synovial recesses does the elbow synovium form?
options: A superior recess above the medial epicondyle
A recess inside the olecranon bursa
An anterior recess corresponding to the coronoid and radial fossae
A posterior recess related to the olecranon fossa
An inferior (annular) recess surrounding the radial neck
questions.explanation: Anterior, posterior and inferior (annular) recesses. The olecranon bursa is a separate periarticular structure.

questions.stem: About the movements of the elbow:
options: Flexion has a range of 140° to 160°
Supination has a range of 70°
Extension has a range of 0°
Pronation occurs at the humero-ulnar joint only
Pronation has a range of 85°
questions.explanation: Pronation-supination occur at the humeroradial and proximal and distal radioulnar joints (radius mobile around a vertical axis). Also false: "Supination has a range of 70°"; "Pronation has a range of 85°".

questions.stem: A patient turns the forearm so that the palm faces upward. This movement is:
options: Supination, range 70°
Pronation, range 85°
Pronation, range 70°
Supination, range 85°
Flexion, range 140°
questions.explanation: Supination rotates the forearm outward, palm up (85°); pronation rotates inward, palm down (70°).

questions.stem: About the posterior palpable landmarks of the elbow:
options: They are the lateral epicondyle, the olecranon and the medial epicondyle
In flexion they form Nélaton's triangle
In flexion they form a straight line
In extension they form Nélaton's triangle
In extension they form Malgaigne's line
questions.explanation: Flexion → Nélaton's triangle; extension → straight line of Malgaigne.

options: Is part of the elbow joint cavity
Reduces friction between soft tissues and the bony prominence
Is a ligament of the elbow
Is a periarticular structure
Secretes the synovial fluid of the elbow joint
questions.explanation: Bursae are periarticular structures reducing friction; the joint's synovial fluid is secreted by the synovium.
